claim: Per the NIST (US) homeowner guide, lightning rods are intended to protect the structure of the house and avoid fires; they do not prevent surges from happening in the wiring.
quote: Note also that lightning rods are intended to protect the structure of the house and avoid fires. They do not prevent surges from happening in the wiring.

claim: Per NIST (US), surge protective devices neither suppress nor arrest a surge; they simply divert it to ground.
quote: What these protective devices do is neither suppress nor arrest a surge, but simply divert it to ground, where it can do no harm.

claim: Per NIST (US), when the protective element of a surge protector fails, the internal disconnect works in one of two ways depending on the design: some protectors cut off the output power completely, others disconnect the failed element but keep the output powered.
quote: depending on the design of the surge protector: some will completely cut-off the output power, others will disconnect the failed element but maintain the power output.

claim: Per NIST (US), a surge protector at the service (breaker) panel is intended to protect all appliances in the house with one device, perhaps supplemented by a few plug-in protectors next to the most sensitive appliances.
quote: The idea is that with one device, all appliances in the house can be protected, perhaps with a few plug-in protectors next to the most sensitive appliances.

claim: Per NIST (US), fitting a snap-in panel surge protector means removing the panel front with the main breaker turned off; the homeowner should check whether local authorities allow them to do it, or hire a licensed electrician.
quote: To install the snap-in protector, you must remove the front panel (do turn off the main breaker before you do that !). Most cities have codes allowing the home owner to do it, under some conditions. Check with your local authorities to find out if they allow you to do that, or hire a licensed electrician to do the installation for you.

claim: Per NIST (US), a detached house with the power drop and the telephone and/or cable TV drops at opposite ends of the house is the worst possible arrangement of the utilities for surge problems.
quote: Detached house with power and telephone and/or cable TV drops at opposite ends of the house - the worst possible arrangement of all.

claim: The US National Electrical Code requires the two incoming services (power and communications) to be properly bonded by a grounding conductor; NIST notes that the opposite-ends arrangement is often made worse by an unintentional violation of this.
quote: worse by a violation (not intentional) of the prescriptions of the National Electrical Code that require that the two incoming services be properly bonded by a grounding conductor.

claim: Per NIST (US), pulling out the power cord of an appliance that stays connected to a telephone line or cable TV might not be the best idea, because the appliance loses the grounding normally provided by the power cord.
quote: pulling out the power cord of an appliance that remains connected to a telephone line or cable TV might not be the best idea: you would lose the grounding of the appliance normally done by the power cord

claim: Per NIST (US), equipment connected to both power and a communications system can be damaged by a surge on either system because of the voltage difference between the two systems during the surge, and this can happen even when each system has its own surge protector.
quote: a surge coming in from one of the two systems - power or communications - can damage the appliance, because of a difference in the voltage between the two systems when the surge occurs. This can happen even when there are surge protectors on each of the systems.

claim: Per NIST (US), the simple solution for equipment with both power and communications connections is a special surge protector that combines, in one package, input/output connections for both systems.
quote: A simple solution to the problem of voltage differences for two-link appliances is to install a special surge protector that incorporates, in the same package, a combination of input/output connections for the two systems.

claim: Per NIST (US), with a combined protector each link (power and communications) is fed through the protector, which is inserted between the wall receptacles and the inputs of the appliance to be protected.
quote: Each link, power and communications, is fed through the protector which is then inserted between the wall receptacles and the input of the appliance to be protected.

claim: Per NIST (US), some combined power/communications plug-in protectors might not work very well if plugged into a 2-blade (ungrounded) receptacle through a 'cheater' plug.
quote: Some of these combined protectors might not work very well if plugged into a 2-blade receptacle, using a "cheater" plug.

claim: Per NIST (US), telephone companies generally provide a surge protector at the point where the telephone line enters the house.
quote: the general practice of telephone companies is to provide a surge protector as part of their services at the point where the telephone line enters the house

claim: Per NIST (US), for a well pump outside the house, a surge protector similar to those used at the power service entrance should be installed at the point where the power line to the pump leaves the house.
quote: The second protection should be provided by a surge protector installed at the point where the power line to the pump leaves the house, using protectors similar to those applied at the power line service entrance.

claim: Per NIST (US), the sensor wiring of a wired intruder alarm runs to all points of the house and acts as an antenna collecting energy from the field of a nearby lightning strike; protection should be part of the system design rather than added later by the owner.
quote: The wires necessary for this type of installation extend to all points of the house and act as an antenna system that collects energy from the field generated by the lightning strike, and protection should be included in the design of the system, rather than added later by the owner.

claim: Per NIST (US, 120 V systems), many plug-in protector specifications show a 330 V clamping voltage, which is not a requirement; somewhat higher clamping voltages such as 400 V or more may be sufficient for protecting electronic appliances.
quote: Many specifications show 330 volts for this voltage. This number is embedded in the UL standard values, but it is not a requirement. Somewhat higher clamping voltages, such as 400 volts or more, may be sufficient for protecting electronic appliances

claim: Per NIST (US), a plug-in surge protector may benefit other receptacles on the same branch circuit, but the benefit is much less on other branch circuits.
quote: If a surge protector is installed on a particular branch circuit, the other receptacles on the same branch circuit might benefit from it, but that benefit is much less on other branch circuits.

claim: Per NIST (US), a surge protector at the service entrance is sufficient for appliances with a single (power-only) connection but not for appliances connected to two systems (power plus communications).
quote: There are two answers to that question: Yes for one-link appliances, No for two-link appliances.

claim: Per NIST (US), an important function of a service-entrance surge protector is to divert large surges arriving on the power line before they enter the house.
quote: An important function of the service-entrance protector is to divert large surges coming on the power line, before they enter the house.

claim: Per NIST (US), specialists consider that most of the (rare) catastrophic failures of surge protectors are caused by excessively high line voltage occurring during a power-system fault, rather than by very large surges.
quote: most of the observed (and quite rare) catastrophic failures of surge protectors are caused by excessively high line voltage that can occur when there is a fault on the power system.

claim: Per NIST (US), a surge protector wired at the service panel should be located close to the panel, less than about 30 cm (one foot), otherwise its voltage-limiting effect is degraded.
quote: The protector should be located close to the service panel (less than about 30 cm or one foot), otherwise the voltage-limiting effect will be degraded.

claim: Per NIST (US), surge current flowing from the telephone entry protector to the common grounding point creates a magnetic field that couples into the loop formed by the power branch circuit, the telephone premises wiring and the bonding conductors, inducing a voltage between the power input and telephone input of the connected PC.
quote: This current produces a magnetic field that couples into the loop formed by the power branch circuit, the telephone premises wiring lines to the PC, and the bonding conductors. A voltage (Vdiff) is induced in the loop and appears across the power input and telephone input of the PC, with upsetting or damaging consequences.

claim: Per NIST (US), another way to reduce the shift in reference potentials is an integrated multi-utility surge protection device at the breaker panel covering AC power, telephone and cable TV with minimum bonding length.
quote: This device includes appropriate surge protection for all three services: AC power, telephone, and cable TV, with the minimum length for the bonding arrangement.

claim: An IT system is not permitted for a low-voltage public supply in the UK because the source is not directly earthed; TN-C and IT systems are both very uncommon in the UK.
quote: IT system is not permitted for a low voltage public supply in the UK because the source is not directly earthed. Therefore TN-C and IT systems are both very uncommon in the UK.

claim: Per UK guidance (IET), earth rods should be driven into virgin ground, not disturbed (backfilled) ground.
quote: they should be driven into virgin ground, not disturbed (backfilled) ground.

quote: Where it is necessary to drive two or more rods and connect them together to achieve a satisfactory result, the separation between rods should be at least equal to their combined driven depth to obtain maximum advantage from each rod.

quote: The potential difference increases with height, therefore the longer the down conductor distance, the larger the separation distance

claim: Per a South African trade article on SANS/IEC 62305, on tall structures a calculated separation distance could be as much as 300 cm or 400 cm, which may not be practical to install.
quote: The taller a structure is the more difficult it would be to obtain a separation distance that would be practical to install, (i.e. a calculated separation distance could be as much as 300 cm or 400 cm from the structure).

claim: Per a South African trade article on SANS/IEC 62305, the required separation distance can be maintained by placing air terminals the required distance from conductive elements, by insulating material (GRP), or by High Voltage Impulse (HVI) conductors.
quote: Separation by means of placing the air terminals the required distance away from the conductive elements • Separation of lightning conductors by means of insulating mate- rial - Glass-fibre Reinforced Plastic (GRP) • Separation by means of High Voltage Impulse (HVI) conductors
section: How to maintain the required separation distance

claim: Per a South African trade article on SANS/IEC 62305, where the calculated separation distance cannot be achieved, lightning current arresters should be considered, but only for rooftop structures that are fed only with electrical or data cables.
quote: Use of lightning current arresters: In cases where the calculated separation distance cannot be achieved, the use of lightning current arresters should be considered. This approach only applies for rooftop structures that are only fed with electrical or data cables.
section: When can separation distances be ignored?

claim: ITU-T K.66 states that overvoltage protection requires bonding metallic services and cable screens to the building earth and installing SPDs at the building entry point on both the power and the telecommunication conductors.
quote: To provide this protection, it is necessary to bond metallic services and screens to the building earth and install SPDs at the building entry point on power and telecommunication conductors.

claim: ITU-T K.66 lists as good practice for all installations that every earth point is bonded to the main earth bar (possibly via added earth bars) and that nothing is connected to a separate earth electrode that is not bonded to the main earth bar.
quote: Bond all earths points to the main earth bar (MEB). This may be via added earth bars. Do not connect to a separate earth electrode which is not bonded to the MEB.

claim: ITU-T K.66 notes that associated equipment whose ports have a low surge impedance to ground and that is connected by short cables (example given: printers on USB cables) may be damaged by circulating earth currents.
quote: Associated equipment containing ports with a low surge impedance to ground connected by short cables, e.g., printers using USB cables, may be susceptible to damage due to circulating earth currents.

claim: ITU-T K.66 says conducted energy entering on services is mitigated by connecting all services with low-impedance bonding conductors to the main earth terminal (MET), mesh bonding network or common bonding network, and that low impedance is obtained by keeping bonding conductors shorter than 1.5 m.
quote: The penetration of conducted energy is mitigated by interconnecting all with low-impedance bonding conductors to the MET, the mesh bonding network or CBN. This low impedance is achieved by keeping the length of bonding conductors short (< 1.5 m).

claim: ITU-T K.66 explains that its 1.5 m limit for bonding conductors is based on an assumed voltage drop of 1 kV per metre of conductor length during direct lightning strikes.
quote: The limit value of 1.5 m for connecting conductors is based on an assumed voltage drop on such conductors, U = 1 kV per m length, for direct lightning strikes.

claim: ITU-T K.66 Table 8-1 gives the maximum bonding conductor length as 1.5 m where direct strikes are the mechanism and 10 m for induced surges, and a maximum resistance of 1 ohm for power induction/power contact.
quote: Direct strikes 1.5 m Induced surges 10 m Power induction/power contact 1 Ω (< 50 V a.c. @ 2 times 24 A a.c.)

claim: ITU-T K.66 recommends that all metallic services (a.c. mains, telecommunication cables, gas and water pipes, CATV) and the earthing conductor enter the building at the same point, to shorten bonding conductors and reduce EMI.
quote: It is recommended that all metallic services, e.g., a.c. mains power, telecommunication cables, gas pipes, water pipes, CATV and the earthing conductor enter the building at the same point to reduce bonding conducting lengths and to reduce EMI.

claim: Where services enter at different points, ITU-T K.66 requires an earthed equipotential bonding bar or bonding terminal near each entry point, each connected to an earthing system, with all the bonding bars bonded together, for example by a ring conductor.
quote: Each EBB or BT shall be connected to an earthing system and all the EBBs shall be bonded together, for example by a ring conductor

claim: ITU-T K.66 warns that national safety regulations may prohibit using a metallic water pipe as the main earth terminal.
quote: Note that national safety regulations may prohibit the use of the metallic waterpipe as the MET.

claim: ITU-T K.66 says the shields of all cables entering the building should be bonded directly to the main earth terminal or equipotential bonding bar; an SPD may be used instead to give galvanic isolation if corrosion requires it.
quote: the shields of all cables entering the building should be directly bonded to the MET or the EBB. SPDs may be used for galvanic isolation, if necessary for corrosion considerations.

claim: Where short bond wires cannot be installed, ITU-T K.66 allows using the shortest possible bond wires plus additional SPDs at the equipment to achieve bonding there, and these additional SPDs must be coordinated with the upstream SPDs.
quote: install the shortest bond wires possible and use additional SPDs, e.g., CPUs, see clause 10, to achieve bonding at the equipment. These additional SPDs shall be coordinated with the upstream SPDs.

claim: ITU-T K.66 notes that equipment without an earth connection in a building with a non-metallic floor can suffer a discharge during a direct strike, because the earth potential rise at the equipment location can differ from that at the main earth terminal.
quote: Equipment without an earth connection is installed in a building with a non-metallic floor. Under direct strike conditions, the earth potential rise at the location of the equipment can be different to that of the location of the MET, resulting in a discharge to the equipment.

claim: ITU-T K.66 recommends that mains SPDs (primary protectors) be placed where their connecting leads to the mains conductors, including the neutral, are as short as possible, with lead lengths below 0.5 m.
quote: The SPD should be located where the leads for connection to the mains conductors, including the neutral conductor, where applicable, are as short as possible. Lead lengths that are less than 0.5 m are recommended.

claim: ITU-T K.66 says that locating the telecommunication primary protectors near the power mains entrance lets the earthing conductor from protector to main earth terminal be kept under 1.5 m, and that this short, low-impedance conductor reduces surge voltage differences between the telecom lines and the power system protective conductor.
quote: By also locating these primary protectors near the entrance of the power mains, the length of the earthing conductor from the protector to the MET can be kept < 1.5 metres. The low impedance of a short earthing conductor helps to reduce surge voltage differences between the telecommunication lines and the protective conductor of the power system.

claim: ITU-T K.66 warns that earthing telecommunication primary protectors only to a separate earth electrode is not compatible with protecting equipment and may even cause a fire in the premises or injury or death of a person using telecommunication equipment.
quote: the earthing terminal of the telecommunication line primary protectors is connected only to a separate earth electrode. This is not compatible with protecting the equipment and it may even result in a fire in the premises or, injury or death of a person using telecommunication equipment in the premises.

claim: ITU-T K.66 says additional SPDs such as multiservice SPDs are sometimes installed at the terminal equipment to limit surges coupled inside the building, and their common terminal should be connected to the protective conductor near the protected equipment.
quote: Additional SPDs, e.g., MSPD, are sometimes installed at the location of the telecommunication terminal equipment in order to limit surges caused by coupling within the building. The common terminal of these protectors should be connected to the protective conductor near the protected equipment.

claim: ITU-T K.66 warns that a telecommunication primary protector installed inside the premises creates a fire risk from overheated wiring, SPD or SPD housing if lightning strikes the telecom service line directly or the line contacts a power conductor.
quote: If a primary protector is installed inside the premises, there is a risk of a fire occurring, due to overheated telecommunication wiring, SPD or SPD housing, if a direct lightning strike occurs to the telecommunication service cable/line or there is a contact between the telecommunication service cable/line and a power conductor.

claim: ITU-T K.66 describes multiservice surge protective devices (MSPDs) as containing the SPDs for all ports, achieving the short-bond-wire requirement, being installed near the equipment so they also protect against overvoltages arising in internal wiring, and requiring coordination with the primary protector.
quote: MSPDs contain the SPDs for all ports and achieve the requirement for short bond wires. They are installed near the equipment and hence also protect against overvoltages occurring in internal wiring. MSPDs shall be coordinated with the primary protector.

claim: ITU-T K.66 cautions that indiscriminate use of MSPDs may allow damage to the protected equipment and to associated equipment.
quote: The indiscriminate use of MSPDs may allow damage to occur to the equipment being protected and associated equipment.

claim: Per ITU-T K.66, a single MSPD suits one piece of equipment or interconnected equipment in close proximity, and in that case only the ports connected to external cables need protection.
quote: This method is suitable for protection of a single piece of equipment and for protecting interconnected equipment in close proximity. In this case, only ports connected to external cables require protection.

claim: Per ITU-T K.66, multiple MSPDs are needed when interconnected equipment is too far apart to share one MSPD (or it has too few outlets), and in that case all ports require protection.
quote: This method needs to be used when the interconnected equipment is spaced too far apart, e.g., the power cord of one piece of equipment will not reach the MSPD, or there are insufficient outlets on the MSPD. In this case all ports require protection.

claim: ITU-T K.66 says that where a customer installation consists of several buildings and the telecom cable continues from the first building to the others, the telecommunications equipment of each building should be earthed and protected as for an individual building.
quote: Some installations at customers' premises may consist of several buildings, with the telecommunications cable from the public network entering the first building then continuing to the other buildings. In that case, the telecommunications equipment of each building should be earthed and protected as in the previous case for an individual building.

claim: ITU-T K.66 Annex A notes that a mains SPD may be installed before or after the earth leakage breaker, but installing it after may cause nuisance tripping, particularly if the breaker contains an RCD.
quote: The SPD may be installed before the ELB (option 1) or after the ELB (option 2). If option 2 is used, nuisance tripping of the circuit breaker may occur, particularly if it contains an RCD.

claim: ITU-T K.66 Annex A figure notes specify that the total length of SPD connecting wires should be under 0.5 m and the total length of bonding plus connecting wires from the SPD to the main earth terminal should be under 1.5 m.
quote: NOTE 2 – Total length of SPD connecting wires should be as short as possible (< 0.5 m). NOTE 3 – Total length of bonding and connecting wires (SPD to MET) should be as short as possible (< 1.5 m).

claim: ITU-T K.66 Appendix I states that of five identified customer earthing/bonding practices, only the common earth bar with short bond wires protects equipment from surges entering via external cables without additional protection.
quote: Only practice 1, shown in Figure I.1, will protect the equipment without the use of additional protection from overvoltage surges entering via external cables.

claim: ITU-T K.66 gives the example that, without a common bonding point with short conductors, a 50 A surge from the telecom line discharging through a 300 ohm earth electrode raises the telecommunication equipment 15 kV above the power network.
quote: a 50-A surge from the telecommunication line discharging to ground via a 300-Ω earth electrode will cause a 15-kV earth potential rise of the telecommunication equipment with respect to the power network.

claim: ITU-T K.66 Appendix II lists metal-free fibre optic cables for signal links between Class I equipment as a mitigation measure in existing TN-C or TN-C-S installations.
quote: mitigation measures (either one alone or in combination) may be applied: 1) metal-free fibre optic cables for signal links interconnecting Class I equipment;

claim: ITU-T K.85 defines a multiservice surge protective device (MSPD) as an SPD containing both telecommunications and mains protection, which may also include port protection for video or Ethernet.
quote: A surge protective device (SPD) containing both telecommunications and mains protection. It may also include port protection for video or Ethernet.

claim: ITU-T K.85 states that if an internal equipment port is subjected to conducted lightning surges or a.c. surges there will be equipment damage and human safety issues, so correct classification of ports matters.
quote: Correct classification of ports is important. If an internal port is subject to conducted lightning surges or a.c. surges, there will be equipment damage and human safety issues.

claim: ITU-T K.85 warns that extending a service to an outbuilding is a problem because equipment designed for intra-building cabling may have insufficient safety isolation and insufficient overvoltage resistibility when connected to inter-building cables.
quote: A problem then occurs if the network operator, or the customer, decides to extend the service to an outbuilding. Equipment designed for connection to intra-building cabling may have insufficient isolation from the point of view of safety and insufficient resistibility to overvoltages, when connected to inter-building cables.

claim: ITU-T K.85 lists non-bonded earths, difficulty installing SPDs at the building entry, and bonding wires longer than 10 m as examples of non-compliance with ITU-T K.66.
quote: Non-compliance with [ITU-T K.66] could include: • non-bonded earths; • difficulty in installing SPDs at the building entry; • bonding wires in excess of 10 m.

claim: ITU-T K.85 identifies four equipment earthing methods: no earthing, earthing via the mains plug, hard-wired bonding to protective earth, and connection to a stand-alone earthing system/electrode.
quote: There are four methods of earthing and these are: 1) no earthing; 2) earthing via the mains plug (i.e., connection to protective earth); 3) hard-wire earthing (i.e., direct bonding to protective earth); 4) connection to a stand-alone earthing system/electrode.

claim: ITU-T K.85 says its earthing method 4 (a stand-alone earthing system/electrode) is most likely unsuitable for customer premises equipment because of the consequences of not being bonded to protective earth.
quote: Method 4 is most likely not suitable for customer premises equipment due to the consequences of a lack of bonding to protective earth.

claim: ITU-T K.85 says that, regardless of the risk assessment result, a building with a lightning protection system should have primary protection bonded to protective earth at the point of entry for all services, and all metallic pipes bonded to protective earth at the point of entry.
quote: Regardless of the risk assessment result, if the building has a lightning protection system (LPS) installed, primary protection, bonded to the protective earth (PE), should be installed at the point of entry for all services; and all metallic pipes should be bonded to the PE at the point of entry.

claim: For internal cable interfaces, ITU-T K.85 considers the risk quite low when the equipment at one end of the cable has a level of insulation, i.e. no earth and no power connection.
quote: The equipment at one end on the cable has a level of insulation, i.e., no earth and no power connection. In this case the risk can be considered quite low.

claim: For external cable interfaces, ITU-T K.85 says to install an MSPD if the risk from flashes near the service line is unacceptable, and also SPDs at the point of entry if the risk from flashes to the service line is unacceptable.
quote: If the risk of damage to the external cable interface, due to flashes near the service line, is above acceptable levels, install an MSPD. If the risk of loss due to flashes to the service line is above acceptable levels, also install SPDs at the point of entry.

claim: ITU-T K.85 summarises the two-stage scheme as: the MSPD protects the equipment and the primary (point-of-entry) protection protects the MSPD, both installed according to ITU-T K.66 when the risk assessment requires.
quote: When required by the risk assessment, MSPDs and primary protection should be installed according to [ITU-T K.66]. The MSPD protects the equipment and the primary protection protects the MSPD.

claim: ITU-T K.85 warns that the MSPDs it refers to rely on a protective earth connection for safety, and that without a protective earth users may be exposed to surges exceeding a few hundred volts; incorrect use of MSPDs may increase the probability of damage.
quote: Incorrect use of MSPDs may actually increase the probability of damage. NOTE – The type of MSPD referred to in this Recommendation relies on a protective earth connection for safety. If used without a protective earth users may be exposed to surges exceeding a few hundred volts.

claim: ITU-T K.85 names wireless links within the home network as a method of protection and says an optical fibre solution could also be used.
quote: Operators can provide a wireless service to provide communication within the home network. This is a method of protection. An optical fibre solution could also be used.
section: 6.9 Use of wireless and optical fibre

claim: ITU-T K.85 notes that if two separate earth electrodes are not bonded together, a potential difference may arise between them and damage the ports of the equipment connected to each; a ring earth is offered as a solution.
quote: Unless these are bonded together, a potential difference may occur between the electrodes and damage the ports of equipment A and equipment B. A ring earth can be a solution for equipotentialization

claim: ITU-T K.85 says an MSPD protects equipment against surges magnetically coupled into building wiring and service lines, and may give some protection against direct strikes to the service plant only if the strike point is more than a few hundred metres from the building.
quote: An MSPD can protect the equipment against surges magnetically coupled into the building wiring and service cables and lines. It may also provide some level of protection of the equipment against direct strikes to the service plant, provided the strike point is more than a few hundred metres from the building.

claim: ITU-T K.85 Annex B lists connecting an internal port to an external cable as a damaging practice; the remedies are to use an external interface, install an SPD to IEC 61643-21/-22, or use an isolation box.
quote: a) Internal port connected to an external cable. The solutions are: i. connect the external cable to an external interface; ii. install an SPD according to [IEC 61643-21] and [IEC 61643-22]; iii. use an isolation box to provide the necessary isolation.

claim: ITU-T K.85 Annex B states that when an internal port connects to associated equipment in the same building that is bonded to a separate earth system, all earth references must be bonded to the same point, usually the protective earth, to prevent damage.
quote: the associated equipment is bonded to a separate earth system. To prevent damage, all earth references must be bonded to the same point, usually the PE.

claim: ITU-T K.85 Annex B lists as a damaging practice an internal port connected to an internal cable that has a gas discharge tube bonded to a separate earth; the stated solution is to remove the GDT.
quote: e) Internal port is connected to internal cable which has a gas discharge tube (GDT), bonded to a separate earth connected to it. The solution is: • remove the GDT.

claim: In the ITU-T K.85 worked risk example, the Ethernet-port damage calculation was based on a vertical loop and a 1 kV withstand voltage, which the document calls most likely a worst case, so it assumed the Ethernet port would not need protection.
quote: However, the calculation FM is based on a vertical loop and a withstand voltage of 1 kV. This is most likely a worst-case situation and it is expected that damage to the Ethernet ports will be lower than indicated in the table. Therefore, it is assumed the Ethernet port will not need protection.

claim: ITU-T K.85 notes that in an optical fibre service, a lightning strike to the fibre cable's metallic tracer/locate wire may damage equipment, depending on how that wire is terminated.
quote: For example, depending on the method of terminating the optical fibre tracer/locate wire, a strike to the wire may cause damage to equipment.

claim: ITU-T K.85 notes that earthed equipment can suffer internal-port damage because surge current returning to the main earth terminal through the earth wire makes the equipment rise in potential.
quote: There is a possibility of damage to the internal port due to current returning to the MET via the earth wire causing the equipment to rise in potential.

claim: ITU-T K.85 says adding an MSPD with protection for all ports provides equipotential bonding for non-earthed equipment, and protection of equipment and users should be effective if the MSPD is plugged into an earthed power point.
quote: Adding an MSPD with protection for all ports will provide equipotential bonding. If the MSPD is plugged into an earthed power point, protection of the equipment and its users should be effective.

claim: ITU-T K.85 warns that if the power point feeding an MSPD is not earthed, equipment damage may not be reduced and users face a possible lightning safety risk because the mains SPDs breach the double-insulated mains transformer.
quote: If the power point is not earthed, equipment damage levels may not be reduced and a possible safety risk for users exists for lightning as the mains double insulation transformer will be breached by the main SPDs.

claim: ITU-T K.85 notes that if protection is needed for ports on long internal cables it may also be needed for ports on short cables, and suggests always assuming a 10 m² loop area for Ethernet ports in the risk assessment.
quote: If the risk assessment indicates that protection is needed for ports connected to long internal cables, protection may also be required for ports connected to short cables. It is suggested to always use a loop area of 10 m² for Ethernet ports.
section: Appendix II.5 Consideration of loop areas

claim: ITU-T K.85 says that for earthed equipment the risk of internal-port damage from mains surge current requires either a mains primary protector or connecting all ports, external and internal, through an MSPD.
quote: Risk of damage on internal ports due to mains current requires either mains primary protector or all ports (external and internal) to connect via an MSPD.

claim: ITU-T K.71 covers two antenna cases when direct-strike protection is required: an antenna on the building, and an antenna on a mast near the building at a maximum distance of about ten metres.
quote: 1) The antenna is located on the building. 2) The antenna is installed on a mast near to the building at a maximum distance of about ten metres.

claim: Per ITU-T K.71, when the risk of loss of human life for the building with its antenna is below the tolerable risk, the site is considered inherently protected against direct lightning and the antenna need only be protected against mains contact.
quote: When the risk R1 of the building, with the antenna installation, is less than the tolerable risk RT1, the site is considered inherently protected against direct lightning. In this case, the antenna need only be protected against mains contact (clause 8.2).

claim: ITU-T K.71 warns that contact between an antenna or its cabling and a phase conductor can cause fire from overheating or electric shock; protection is by bonding the antenna system to the main earthing bar or by adequate isolation.
quote: Contact between the antenna or associated cabling and a phase conductor can cause serious problems, e.g., a fire due to overheating or electric shock. Protection can be provided by either bonding the antenna system to the MEB or by providing adequate isolation.

claim: ITU-T K.71 treats a minimum 3 m horizontal clearance between an antenna installation (and its lead-in cable) and aerial power line conductors as conservative.
quote: Maintaining suitable clearance distances of the antenna installation (and associated lead-in cable) from aerial line conductors. A minimum 3 m horizontal clearance would be considered conservative.

claim: ITU-T K.71 says the antenna lead-in cable should not cross over or under overhead mains power service lines.
quote: The antenna lead-in cable should not cross over or under overhead mains power service lines.

claim: ITU-T K.71 says that where adequate isolation of an antenna installation from mains conductors cannot be maintained, the installation should be bonded to the building earthing system.
quote: Where it is not possible to maintain adequate isolation, the installation should be bonded to the building earthing system, see clause 8.2.1.

claim: ITU-T K.71 prohibits installing antennas on buildings whose roofs are covered with highly flammable materials such as thatch or reed-like material.
quote: Antennas shall not be installed on buildings having roofs covered with highly flammable materials (for example, thatch, reed-like material, etc.).

claim: ITU-T K.71 requires that where a building has a lightning protection system, the antenna system is either bonded to the LPS or adequately isolated or insulated from it.
quote: When there is an LPS, the antenna system must either be bonded to the LPS or be adequately isolated or insulated from the LPS.

claim: Where an antenna is to be bonded to an existing LPS, ITU-T K.71 says to bond the antenna mast to the building's LPS and electrical safety earthing system.
quote: Bond the antenna mast to the building's LPS and electrical safety earthing system as shown in Figure 6.

claim: ITU-T K.71 says that for an antenna not bonded to the LPS, a 2 m clearance from LPS components including down conductors should be adequate for buildings of one or two storeys.
quote: If the antenna is not bonded to the LPS, it is necessary to ensure adequate separation between the antenna installation and the LPS components, including the down conductors. For buildings of one or two storeys, a 2 m clearance should be adequate.
section: 9.2.2.2 Antenna not bonded to the LPS

claim: For an antenna on a mast near the building where lightning protection is not required (R1 ≤ RT1), ITU-T K.71 says protection may only be needed for electrical safety and it is not necessary to bond the tower earth electrode system to the building electrical installation earth.
quote: In this situation, lightning protection is not required, and protection may only be required for electrical safety, see clause 8.2. In this case, it is not necessary to bond the tower earth electrode system to the building electrical installation earth.

claim: For an antenna mast near the building where lightning protection is required (R1 > RT1), ITU-T K.71 lists among the required measures that the coaxial cable outer conductor is bonded to the bonding bar at the entrance of the building.
quote: the outer conductor of the coaxial cable is bonded to the BB at the entrance of the building (see Figure 7);

claim: ITU-T K.71 lists installing one or two parallel earthing conductors (PEC), in general connected to the mast and building earthing systems, as a measure whose resistance must reduce the lightning current flowing into the coaxial-cable SPD to the required value.
quote: installing one or two parallel earthing conductors (PEC). The resistance value of the PEC shall reduce the lightning current flowing into the SPD to the required value. In general, the PEC, or other protective measure, should be connected to the mast and building earthing systems;

claim: ITU-T K.71 requires an antenna mast bonding conductor to be installed straight and vertical so that it gives the shortest, most direct path to the LPS or building earthing system.
quote: The bonding conductor shall be installed straight and vertical such that it can provide the shortest, most direct path to the LPS or building earthing system.

claim: ITU-T K.71 requires the outer conductors of all coaxial cables from the antenna to be connected to the antenna mast or the building earthing system through an equipotential bonding conductor of specified minimum cross-section, avoiding loops.
quote: The outer conductors of all coaxial cables coming from the antenna shall be connected to the antenna mast or to the building earthing system via an equipotential bonding conductor having a minimum cross-section as specified below. The formation of loops shall be avoided.

claim: ITU-T K.71 forbids using the electricity supply's protective earth and/or neutral conductors, or the outer conductor of any coaxial cable, as the antenna bonding conductor; a dedicated bonding conductor must be used.
quote: The following shall not be used as a bonding conductor, i.e., a specific bonding conductor shall be used: – protective earth and/or neutral conductors of the electricity supply; – the outer conductor of any coaxial cable.

claim: Per ITU-T K.71, an antenna bonding conductor intended to carry the full lightning current to ground should, if bare, have a cross-section of at least 14 mm2 copper, 22 mm2 aluminium or 50 mm2 steel.
quote: Bonding to safely discharge to ground the full lightning current In this case, a suitable bare conductor would have a minimum cross-sectional area of not less than 14 mm2 Cu, 22 mm2 Al or 50 mm2 Fe.

claim: Per ITU-T K.71, a full-lightning-current antenna bonding conductor that is insulated, enclosed (e.g. in concrete) or close to flammable material needs at least 35 mm2 copper, 55 mm2 aluminium or 125 mm2 steel.
quote: If this conductor is insulated, enclosed (e.g., by concrete) or close to flammable material, a minimum cross-sectional area of not less than 35 mm2 Cu, 55 mm2 Al or 125 mm2 Fe would be required.

claim: Per ITU-T K.71, an antenna bonding conductor intended to carry only a partial lightning current should have a cross-section of at least 5 mm2 copper, 8 mm2 aluminium or 16 mm2 steel.
quote: Bonding to safely discharge to ground a partial lightning current In this case a suitable bonding conductor would have a minimum cross-sectional area of not less than 5 mm2 Cu, 8 mm2 Al or 16 mm2 Fe.

claim: ITU-T K.71 notes that, for the protective conductor bonding an antenna system to the main earth terminal against mains contact, compliance with IEC 60364-5-54 can in most cases be achieved with at least 2.5 mm2 copper (16 mm2 aluminium) if mechanically protected, or 4 mm2 copper (16 mm2 aluminium) if not.
quote: In most cases, compliance with [IEC 60364-5-54] can be achieved by using a protective conductor with a cross-sectional area not less than: • 2.5 mm2 Cu or 16 mm2 Al, if protection against mechanical damage is provided; • 4 mm2 Cu or 16 mm2 Al, if protection against mechanical damage is not provided.

claim: Where an LPS is required, ITU-T K.71 (citing IEC 62305-3) gives one acceptable earth electrode arrangement as at least two horizontal electrodes each at least 2.5 m long, at an angle larger than 60°, buried at least 0.5 m deep and no closer than 1 m to the foundation.
quote: a minimum of two horizontal earth electrodes of at least 2.5 m length buried in an angle larger than 60°, at least 0.5 m deep and not closer than 1 m to the foundation; or

claim: Where an LPS is required, ITU-T K.71 (citing IEC 62305-3) alternatively accepts one vertical or inclined earth electrode at least 2.5 m long, or two vertical electrodes at least 1.5 m long spaced 3 m apart, not closer than 1 m to the foundation.
quote: a vertical or inclined earth electrode of at least 2.5 m length or two vertical earth electrodes of at least 1.5 m length with a spacing of 3 m and not closer than 1 m to the foundation.

claim: ITU-T K.71 requires SPDs on mains and telecommunication conductors to be located at their entrance into the building, for example at the main electrical board, connected between the conductors and the bonding bar.
quote: The SPDs on mains and telecommunication conductors shall be located at their entrance into the building, e.g., at the main electrical board, between the conductors and the BB.

claim: ITU-T K.71 states that for antenna-cable overvoltage protection at the point of entry to be effective, the bond wire from the cable screen and SPD to the main earth terminal must be shorter than 1.5 m.
quote: To be effective, the length of the bond wire from the cable screen and SPD to the MET must be < 1.5 m.

claim: ITU-T K.71 Appendix I says that when the antenna mast serves as an LPS air termination, the coaxial cable outer conductor shall be bonded to the antenna mast at one end and to the main earthing terminal at the other end.
quote: The outer conductor of the coaxial cable shall be bonded to the antenna mast at one end and to the main earthing terminal at the other end.

claim: One prerequisite of ITU-T K.71's generic low-risk roof-antenna assessment is that the top of the antenna is attached to the outside of the building, less than 2.5 m above the gutter line and below the peak of the roof.
quote: The top of the antenna is attached to the outside of the building, is less than 2.5 m above the gutter line and below the peak of the roof.

claim: ITU-T K.73 requires connection to the main earthing terminal of both ends of metallic cable screens if high unbalanced currents are expected due to different earthing potentials, with precautions taken to limit such currents.
quote: This Recommendation requires the connection to the main earthing terminal of the following elements: • both ends of metallic cable screens, if high unbalanced currents are expected due to different earthing potentials. Precautions should be taken to limit such currents;

claim: ITU-T K.73 says a building should have a main earthing terminal located as close as possible to the a.c. power and telecommunication cable entrance facilities.
quote: The building should be provided with a main earthing terminal, located as close as possible to the a.c. power and telecommunication cable entrance facilities.

claim: ITU-T K.73 explains that when equipment in different buildings is interconnected, current can flow on the cable screen because of the potential difference between the buildings' earthing systems, damaging the cable or equipment and injuring people.
quote: the current could flow on the cable screen laid for the connection between the equipment due to the potential difference between the earthing systems of the buildings. The current can cause damage to the cable and/or to the equipment, and injury to the people.

claim: ITU-T K.73 recommends a TN-S earthing system for the a.c. power distribution, noting it is specified in the EN 50174 series and EN 50310.
quote: A TN-S earthing system is recommended and is specified in some standards [EN 50174 series] and [EN 50310].

claim: ITU-T K.73 notes that if lightning strikes a building, part of the lightning current flows through the screen of a cable to another building and can damage the cable, the equipment and people.
quote: If the lightning flash strikes a building, a part of the lightning current flows through the cable screen and that can cause damage to the cable, to the equipment and to the people.

claim: One ITU-T K.73 solution for inter-building cables is galvanic isolation: the cable screen is kept isolated from the earthing system, and the cable covering must then withstand the screen-to-earth potential difference produced by faults or lightning.
quote: This solution consists of maintaining the cable screen isolated from the earthing system; in this case, the cable covering shall be able to bear the potential difference between the cable screen and the earthing system produced both by fault or by lightning.

claim: ITU-T K.73 requires an appropriate SPD between the isolated cable screen and earth if the cable covering insulation cannot withstand the expected lightning overvoltage.
quote: If the insulation level of the cable covering cannot withstand the expected lightning overvoltage, an appropriate SPD shall be placed across the screen and the earth.

claim: ITU-T K.73 requires that where a cable screen is bonded at one end and left insulated at the other, the non-earthed end is protected against direct contact and labelled to warn of a potential electric shock risk.
quote: the end of the non-earthed cable has to be protected against direct contact, and a label/mark sign shall be used to indicate that a potential electrical shock risk exists (protection of people).

claim: ITU-T K.73 states that the purpose of a parallel bonding conductor (PBC) is to reduce the current flowing on the inter-building cable screen when there are potential differences between the main earthing terminals.
quote: The purpose of a parallel bonding conductor is to reduce the current flowing on the cable screen in case of potential differences between METs.

claim: ITU-T K.73 states that the cable screen generally cannot act as the parallel bonding conductor because it is not designed to cope with a large current.
quote: Generally, the cable screen cannot act as a parallel bonding conductor because it is not designed to cope with a large current.

claim: ITU-T K.73 does not recommend connecting a metallic cable between two buildings for privately owned telecommunication equipment (e.g. ADSL modem and computer), as it may cause safety or electrical problems.
quote: If the telecommunication equipment between two buildings belongs to a private person (such as ADSL modem and computer), it is not recommended to connect the cable between the two buildings, as it may cause some safety or electrical problems.

claim: For buildings with different earthing and power feeding, ITU-T K.73 calls for the cable screen to be connected to the main earthing terminal at the entrance of each building and for measurement of the possible current between the two METs.
quote: At the entrance of each building, the connection between the cable screen and the MET is requested. Measurement is required in order to access the possible current flowing between the two METs.

claim: ITU-T K.73 says that if the fault-condition current through the cable screen between buildings is unacceptable, a parallel bonding conductor should be routed close to the cable.
quote: In this case, if the current through the cable screen is unacceptable, a parallel bonding conductor (PBC) should be routed closely to the cable.

claim: In ITU-T K.73's appendix on medium-voltage earth faults, a copper parallel bonding conductor of at least 50 mm2 is recommended between the buildings' earthing systems when the potential difference cannot be determined.
quote: When the value of ∆V1 cannot be identified, the copper PBC of minimum size 50 mm2 is recommended to be laid.

claim: ITU-T K.98 distinguishes earthing (connecting the earth bar to earth, usually via an installed electrode) from bonding (interconnecting earth electrodes and metallic parts to minimise potential differences).
quote: Earthing is the connection of the earth bar to earth, usually via an installed earth electrode. Bonding is the interconnection of earth electrodes and metallic parts to minimise potential differences.

claim: ITU-T K.98 says a customer-premises earth electrode could have a resistance to earth anywhere from tens of ohms to hundreds of ohms.
quote: This electrode could have a resistance to earth in the range of tens of Ω to hundreds of Ω.

claim: ITU-T K.98 explains that an auxiliary earth electrode not bonded to the main earth terminal is a problem because surge current in it makes the external telecommunication port rise in potential relative to the MET, which can break down equipment insulation and cause damage and a safety hazard.
quote: The problems with using an auxiliary earth electrode and not bonding it to the MET is that surge current conducted in the auxiliary earth electrode causes the external telecommunication port to rise in potential with respect to the MET. If an insulation path within the equipment breaks down, it may result in damage and safety hazard.

claim: ITU-T K.98 calls it essential that the telecommunication primary protector be bonded to the main earth terminal, preferably by a short bonding conductor.
quote: It is essential that the telecommunication primary protector be bonded to the MET, preferably by a short bonding conductor.

claim: ITU-T K.98 cites IEC 60364-4-44 section 444.5 as recommending that all protective and functional earthing conductors connect to one single main earth terminal and that all earth electrodes associated with a building be interconnected.
quote: Section 444.5 of [IEC 60364-4-44] recommends that all protective and functional earthing conductors should be connected to one single MET. It also recommends that all earth electrodes associated with a building be interconnected.

claim: ITU-T K.98 says it is imperative to connect inter-building cables only to external ports and intra-building cables only to internal ports.
quote: Therefore, it is imperative to only connect inter-building cables to external ports and intra-building cables to internal ports.
section: 6.4 Correct classification and use of ports

claim: For residential buildings, ITU-T K.98 recommends, when protection is required, an MSPD or equivalent to protect equipment clusters plus primary protection at the building entry point to protect the downstream protection and the equipment wiring.
quote: When required, it is recommended that a MSPD, or equivalent protection, be installed to protect equipment clusters and that primary protection be installed at the building entry point to protect the downstream protection and the equipment wiring.

claim: ITU-T K.98 says that, as a result of the coordination requirement in ITU-T K.21, the external telecommunication port only requires a gas discharge tube bonded to the main earth terminal.
quote: As a result of the coordination requirement in [ITU-T K.21], the telecommunication port only requires a GDT bonded to the MET.

claim: ITU-T K.98 warns that particular problems may occur where equipment is connected to equipment in another building on the same site, and refers to ITU-T K.73 for solutions.
quote: Where equipment is connected to other equipment in another building on the same site, particular problems may occur. Refer to [ITU-T K.73] for detailed information and solutions.

claim: ITU-T K.98 says most Ethernet ports have a signal transformer that is generally sufficient against line-to-earth surges, but Power over Ethernet equipment may be more susceptible to damage and may need an engineered protection solution.
quote: Most Ethernet ports have a signal transformer which is generally sufficient to protect the port against line to earth surges. Power over Ethernet (PoE) equipment may be more susceptible to damage and where off the shelf protection is not available, an engineering solution may be needed.

claim: ITU-T K.98 notes that protecting internal ports is not as simple as protecting external ports because internal ports have no coordination requirement; such ports must be protected in accordance with IEC 61643-21 and IEC 61643-22.
quote: Protection of the internal ports is not as simple as external ports as internal ports do not have a coordination requirement. Ports without a coordination requirement must be protected in accordance with [IEC 61643-21] and [IEC 61643-22].

claim: ITU-T K.98 concludes that the ideal installation is class II equipment, with equipment clusters protected by an MSPD and the MSPD protected by primary protection when necessary.
quote: The ideal installation is class II equipment with equipment clusters protected by a MSPD and the MSPD protected by primary protection when necessary.

claim: ITU-T K.98 concludes from its direct-strike simulations that telecommunication equipment not protected by primary protection will always be damaged, except for the combination of a direct strike to a TN-C power system with floating equipment.
quote: For equipment not protected by primary protection Damage will always occur to the telecommunication equipment except for the combination of a direct strike to a TN-C power system with floating equipment.

claim: In ITU-T K.98's simulations, floating (class II) equipment was always protected once primary protection was installed, regardless of the power system type and the earth resistance at the premises.
quote: Floating equipment is always protected by the installation of primary protection, regardless of the power system and the resistance to earth at the customer premises.

claim: In ITU-T K.98 Table 2, for a strike to the telecommunication line with a TN-S power system, earthed equipment with primary protection is listed as protected only for the combination of a 100 ohm customer premises earth and a 1.5 m telecommunication bond wire.
quote: Strike to telecommunication line and a Only protected for: TN-S power system. • the combination of a 100 Ω customer premises earth and a 1.5 m telecommunication bond wire.

claim: ITU-T K.98 notes that in structures relying on a bond to underground metallic services for their path to earth, that path may be missing if plastic pipes have been retrofitted or installed.
quote: In structures relying on a bond to underground services, this path to earth may be missing if plastic pipes have been retrofitted or installed.

claim: In an ITU-T K.98 simulation (lightning strike to a TN-S power system, earthed equipment without primary protection, 100 ohm customer earth), the main earth terminal and the equipment SELV circuit both rose to 63 kV with respect to remote earth, a magnitude that may result in flashovers.
quote: Because of the relatively high resistance to earth, the MET and the SELV circuit voltages with respect to the remote earth and the local earth outside the area of influence of the current entering the earth, both rise to 63 kV. Voltage of this magnitude may result in flashovers.
section: A.2.1.1.1, Figure A.2, customer earth 100 Ω

claim: In an ITU-T K.98 simulation (strike to a TN-S power system, earthed equipment without primary protection) with the earth connection missing from the power outlet, the Ethernet port saw a 3.3 kV peak, exceeding its nominal 2.5 kV breakdown voltage.
quote: The Ethernet port is subjected to a voltage peak of 3.3 kV which exceeds the nominal breakdown voltage of 2.5 kV.
section: A.2.1.1.1, unearthed power outlet and customer earth 100 Ω

claim: In ITU-T K.98 Appendix II's example of earth potential rise around a single rod earth electrode, there can be 70 kV between a cable bonded to the main earth terminal and a point 20 m from the electrode, which the document uses to show the necessity of a ring earth for structures without a bonded reinforced concrete floor.
quote: there can be a voltage of 70 kV between a cable bonded to the MET and a point 20 m from the electrode which can result in a hazardous situation for the people and the property. This shows the necessity for a ring earth for structures without a bonded reinforced concrete floor.

claim: Southwest Microwave's technical note observes that security devices installed outdoors are typically exposed to surges, transients and lightning.
quote: Security devices installed outdoors are typically exposed to surges, transients, and lightning.

claim: For an outdoor PoE security device, Southwest Microwave requires an outdoor-rated surge suppressor with shielded RJ45 connections mounted within 3 feet (0.91 m) of the PoE device; it may need its own enclosure.
quote: Outdoor rated surge suppressor with shielded RJ45 connections. Must be mounted within 3 feet (.91m) of the POE device. (May require enclosure)

claim: Southwest Microwave specifies Cat5e or Cat6 shielded twisted Ethernet cable with shielded RJ45 connectors, not longer than 100 m (328 ft), routed through a permanently earthed metal conduit.
quote: Cat5e or Cat6 shielded twisted Ethernet cable with shielded RJ45 connectors not to exceed 100m (328 ft.). The cable must be routed through a permanently earthed metal conduit.

claim: At the switch end, Southwest Microwave shows a field distribution box containing an outdoor PoE network switch with shielded ports and its own outdoor-rated surge suppressor, in addition to the suppressor at the PoE device.
quote: Field distribution box with outdoor PoE network switch with shielded ports, outdoor rated surge suppressor and any additional infrastructure equipment required.

claim: If the PoE switch is mounted indoors, Southwest Microwave requires a surge suppressor on the outside of the building before the cable enters the building.
quote: if the switch is mounted indoors, a surge suppressor must be mounted on the outside of the building before the cable enters the building.

claim: Southwest Microwave's Figure 1 annotates the earth connections of the surge-suppressor installation simply as 'Earth ground per local code'.

claim: Axis advises using shielded network cable (STP) throughout when installing its network cameras.
quote: equipment if not handled properly. When installing Axis cameras, use shielded network cables (STP) throughout. To benefit from the surge-resistant design

claim: Axis defines a power surge as a transient voltage spike in a power or data line; lightning is the most familiar cause but only one of several.
quote: A power surge is a transient voltage spike in a power or data line. The most familiar cause is lightning strikes, but this is just one of several common reasons.

claim: According to Axis, more frequent surge causes than lightning include the switching on and off of high-powered machinery such as elevator motors or air conditioners.
quote: More frequent causes include the switching on and off of high-powered machinery, such as elevator motors or air conditioners.

claim: Axis explains that the network cable between a camera and its switch can pick up strong magnetic and electric fields nearby, producing voltage transients that travel along the cable.
quote: The network cable connecting the camera to a switch can pick up strong magnetic and electrical fields in its immediate proximity. This could lead to voltage transients propagating along the cable.

claim: With shielded (STP) network cable, Axis says the induced energy is captured by the shield and diverted to ground without reaching the camera.
quote: With a shielded network cable (STP), the electric energy is trapped by the shield instead, and can be diverted to ground without ever reaching the camera.

claim: Axis states the shield only works if it has an unbroken path to ground through the power sourcing equipment (PSE).

claim: Axis warns that a camera on unshielded network cable can be adversely affected by surges caused by strong electromagnetic fields near the cable.

claim: Axis calls proper grounding of the PSE (PoE switch or midspan) imperative for the cable shield to protect the camera.
quote: For this to work, it is imperative that the PSE is properly grounded.

claim: Axis says its PoE midspan should always be plugged into a grounded socket so that the cable shield can function. (The extracted text contains the stray page-header words 'White papers' inside this sentence.)
quote: midspan should always be connected White papers to a grounded socket for the shield to function properly.

claim: Axis notes that a desktop switch may have no ground connection through its power lead, in which case the switch must be grounded separately.
quote: However, a desktop switch may lack a ground connection through the power line. Therefore, the switch needs to be grounded separately.

claim: Where several network cables are joined to reach a camera, Axis requires every cable, patch panel and coupling in the path to be shielded.
quote: network cables together to reach the camera, make sure each cable and all patch panels and couplings are shielded.

claim: Axis describes PoE-compatible surge protectors as diverting surges to ground before they reach the camera while still passing both data and power.
quote: These surge protectors protect the equipment by diverting the surges to ground before they reach the camera, while still allowing the transfer of both data and power.

claim: Axis states that most PoE surge protectors need shielded network cable in order to function properly.
quote: For most surge protectors to function properly, you must use a shielded network cable.

claim: Axis shows that indoor network devices can be protected by a further surge protector placed where the Ethernet cable is about to enter the building.
quote: devices can be protected by another surge protector placed where the Ethernet cable is about to enter the building.

claim: MikroTik requires that towers and masts carrying the shielded cable installation, the antennas and the router itself are all properly grounded.
quote: Shielded cable installation infrastructure (towers and masts), as well as antennas and the router itself, must be properly grounded.

claim: MikroTik requires lightning arresters on all external antenna cables, near or on the antennas, to prevent equipment damage and human injury.
quote: Lightning arresters must be installed on all external antenna cables (near the antennas or on the antennas themselves) to prevent equipment damage and human injury.

claim: MikroTik notes that lightning arresters are not effective unless they are properly grounded.
quote: Note that lightning arresters will not be effective if they are not properly grounded.

claim: MikroTik specifies 2.5-4 mm2 copper wire (AWG 12-14) with corrosion-resistant connectors for grounding its outdoor routers.
quote: Use 2.5-4 mm² Cu (AWG 12–14) wire with corrosion-resistant connectors for grounding.

claim: MikroTik tells installers to make sure the grounding infrastructure they connect to is fully functional and not merely decorative.
quote: Ensure that the grounding infrastructure you use is fully functional (not merely decorative, as seen in some installations).

claim: MikroTik advises using shielded cables with devices that have shielded connectors, because they give better immunity.
quote: For shielded connectors, please use shielded cables as they provide better immunity.

claim: MikroTik says the grounding wire should go from the RouterBOARD's grounding attachment point (where provided) to the base of the tower.
quote: The grounding wire should be connected to the RouterBOARD grounding wire attachment point if such is provided. This wire should then be connected to the base of the tower, ensuring the connection meets grounding standards.

claim: MikroTik allows the antenna's grounding wire to be connected near the RouterBOARD outdoor case and joined to the same grounding wire as the RouterBOARD.
quote: The antenna's grounding wire should be connected near the RouterBOARD outdoor case and can be joined with the same grounding wire used for the RouterBOARD.

claim: MikroTik warns against powering its devices from PoE power sourcing equipment whose positive terminal is connected to protective earth, because it may cause a short circuit and harm the person and the device.
quote: You should not use Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE) with the positive terminal connected to Protective Earth (PE) if it powers a MikroTik device. It may cause a short circuit, harm you and your device.

claim: Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, site earthing systems are needed both for the safety of personnel and for the protection of equipment.

Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, earthing systems must comply with SANS 10142-1 (wiring of premises, low-voltage installations) and be carried out and certified by competent registered persons.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, the supply transformer's earth system must be connected to the high-site earth system.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, nobody should be allowed onto exposed areas of the site or to climb support structures when there is lightning, or lightning is expected, in the area.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, LPS design is complex, needs specialist knowledge and LPS and earthing specialists should be consulted.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, a lightning finial may be needed to protect equipment on top of the structure and should extend at least 1 m above the highest equipment.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, all antenna feeders should be bonded to the tower at the upper and lower ends and earthed at the point of entry into the equipment shelter.

Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, all indoor and outdoor equipment, including antennas, must have individual earthing connections; daisy-chaining of earthing connections is not permitted.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, all lightning protection units (surge protectors) must be earthed at the point of entry into the equipment shelter.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, a low-resistance earthing system, preferably less than 10 ohms, is recommended to minimise dangerous overvoltages.

Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, a single integrated earthing system serving both lightning protection and safety earthing is preferable, and its resistance should then be less than 1 ohm.

Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, where outdoor radio equipment connects to high-value indoor systems, galvanic isolation by an optical fibre link between outdoor and indoor equipment should be seriously considered to stop lightning-induced surges reaching the indoor equipment.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, antennas must be specified with an earthing lug so the antenna can be securely earthed.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, only metal-bodied cable-end connectors should be used on RJ45 cabled connections.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, data connections should be made using only screened twisted pair cable.

Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, surge suppressors and earthing clamps should be fitted to RF, IF, data and power cables and connected by the shortest path to a common site earthing system.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, the earthing cable for individual equipment units should typically be 16 mm2 yellow/green cable.

Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, all cables entering a shelter should pass through a common metallic bulkhead earthed to the site earthing system, with surge arrestors fitted to the bulkhead.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, all cables should be installed in metallic cable trays that are well earthed.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, earth leakage protection devices should be tested once a year.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, the earthing system should be checked once a year to confirm it is intact and its earth impedance has not risen unreasonably.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, all earthing points and earth straps should be inspected once a year for damage, arcing or corrosion and repaired.
Per the South African WAPA high-site guideline, immediately after lightning damage, all earthing points, earth straps and surge protection devices should be inspected and repaired.

Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, a mesh bonding network (mesh-BN) connects all associated equipment (cabinets, frames, racks, trays, pathways) to a bonding grid that is connected at multiple points to the common bonding network.
quote: A bonding network to which all associated equipment (e.g., cabinets, frames, racks, trays, pathways) are connected using a bonding grid, which is connected to multiple points on the common bonding network (formerly known as the signal reference grid).

claim: Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, a mesh-isolated bonding network (mesh-IBN) uses a bonding grid connected to the common bonding network at a single point only.
quote: A bonding network to which all associated equipment (e.g., cabinets, frames, racks, trays, pathways) are connected using a bonding grid, which is connected to a single point on the common bonding network (formerly known as the isolated signal reference grid).

claim: Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, the primary bonding busbar (PBB), formerly called the telecommunications main grounding busbar (TMGB), is bonded by the telecommunications bonding conductor to the building's electrical service equipment ground.
quote: means of the telecommunications bonding conductor, to the buildings service equipment (power) ground (formerly known as the telecommunications main grounding busbar).

claim: Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, the secondary bonding busbar (SBB), formerly the telecommunications grounding busbar (TGB), is the common bonding point for telecommunications equipment in satellite telecommunications rooms.
quote: A common point of connection for telecommunications system and equipment bonding to ground and located in satellite telecommunications rooms (formerly known as the telecommunications grounding busbar).

claim: Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, the bond between the AC equipment ground (ACEG) and the PBB or SBB must be installed by a licensed electrician.

claim: Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, a rack bonding conductor (RBC) must be at least No. 6 AWG, and an RBC must not be used in place of a rack bonding busbar.

claim: Per US DoD guide spec UFGS 27 05 26, cable shields, metal conduit, cable runway or ladder and other metallic cable pathways may not be used in place of a TEBC.

claim: Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), a communications site shall have only one grounding electrode system: AC power, tower, lightning protection, telephone, structural steel and buried metallic piping grounds are all bonded together.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), ground rods should be spaced apart by the sum of their lengths so that their spheres of influence do not overlap.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), ground rods shall have a minimum length of 2.4 m (8 ft.).
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice, citing NFPA 70 Art. 250.56), ground rods shall not be installed closer than 1.8 m (6 ft.) to other ground rods and grounding electrodes.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), the top of a ground rod shall not be cut off when rock prevents it being driven fully.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), buried ground ring conductors shall be 35 mm2 (#2 AWG) or coarser bare solid copper, tinned or un-tinned.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), ground rings shall be buried in direct contact with earth 762 mm (30 in.) deep where possible, or below the frost line if deeper.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), a building ground ring shall be at least 914 mm (3 ft.) from the building foundation and should lie beyond the roof drip line.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice, citing NFPA 70 Art. 250.64), grounding electrode conductors shall be one continuous length, spliced only with listed irreversible compression connectors or exothermic welds.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), grounding conductors of all sizes shall keep a minimum bending radius of 203 mm (8 in.).
Per Motorola R56 (2005), galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals are electrically connected and coupled through an electrolyte such as soil.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), all below-grade grounding electrode system connections shall be exothermically welded or made with listed irreversible high-compression fittings compressed to at least 13.3 tonnes (12 tons).

Per Motorola R56 (2005), for dispersing lightning energy the shape and dimensions of the grounding electrode system matter more than a specific resistance value, although low resistance is generally recommended.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), light-duty 'Type A' sites have a grounding electrode resistance design goal of 25 ohms or less for a single grounding electrode.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), standard-duty 'Type B' sites (e.g. sites with a tower, dispatch centres, repeater sites) have a grounding electrode system resistance design goal as low as practical and not over 10 ohms.
Per Motorola R56 (2005), doubling the length of a ground rod reduces its resistance by approximately 40 % in homogeneous soil.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), each leg of a self-supporting tower shall be bonded to the tower ground ring with 35 mm2 (#2 AWG) or coarser bare solid tinned copper.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), the ground ring encircling an outdoor equipment cabinet shall be installed at least 610 mm (2 ft.) from the cabinet foundation/pad.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), coaxial transmission line ground kits shall be installed at the first point of contact near the antenna.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), coaxial transmission line ground kits shall also be installed near the building, shelter, equipment housing or cabinet entry point (bonded to the external ground bus bar if one is installed).
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), braided grounding conductors shall not be used under any circumstances.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), metallic objects within 1.8 m (6 ft.) of the external grounding electrode system or of a grounded metallic item shall be bonded to it with 16 mm2 (#6 AWG) or coarser conductors.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), each gate shall be bonded to its supporting fence post with a flexible 16 mm2 (#6 AWG) or coarser stranded copper jumper.
Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice, citing NFPA 780), grounding down-conductors from roof-mounted antenna masts shall be 35 mm2 (#2 AWG) or coarser copper for buildings up to 22.9 m (75 ft.) high.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), access points and wireless routers mounted on the side of a building shall be bonded directly to the building's common grounding electrode system with 16 mm2 (#6 AWG) or coarser copper.

Per Motorola R56 (2005, US practice), cable trays shall not be used as a ground bus conductor for equipment.
